concerns.text: The plan proposes running 10,000 Monte Carlo trials on synthetic data with a *fixed* length (≥1,000) and *fixed* Hurst exponent per configuration, then regressing the *aggregate* error rate against the Hurst exponent. This design lacks the necessary variation in sample size (N) to properly estimate the regression slope of error inflation. The theoretical inflation of Type I error in t-tests under long-range dependence is a function of both H and N (specifically, the effective sample size N_eff). By holding N constant, the regression will only have 4 data points (one per H level), making the slope estimate extremely unstable and unable to distinguish between a true H-dependent effect and random noise in the Monte Carlo estimate. The design must vary N or explicitly model the N-H interaction to support the causal claim of 'robustness' across scales.

The preprocessing strategy (ADF test -> differencing if p<0.05, else detrend) introduces a selection bias that invalidates the subsequent dependence quantification. Differencing a series with H=0.8 (long-range dependence) transforms it into a series with H' = H-1 (short-range dependence or anti-persistence), effectively destroying the very signal (long-range dependence) the study aims to measure. If the ADF test fails to reject the null (p≥0.05) for a series that actually has long-range dependence but no unit root, the plan applies detrending, which may not remove the long-memory component. The plan conflates 'unit root' (I(1)) with 'long-range dependence' (fractional integration). The methodology must distinguish between removing a stochastic trend (unit root) and preserving the fractional integration parameter (H) for the robustness test. Applying differencing to long-memory series will artificially lower the observed H and mask the true error inflation.

The plan states: 'Regression of Observed Error Rate vs. Hurst Exponent' with 'Hurst exponent ONLY' as a predictor. However, the theoretical variance inflation factor (VIF) for a t-test under long-range dependence is a function of the sample size N and the autocorrelation structure. If N is fixed (as implied by the synthetic generation step 'Length ≥ 1,000'), the regression of error rate vs. H is valid *only if* the error rate is the dependent variable. But the plan also mentions calculating 'Effective Sample Size (N_eff)'. If N_eff varies significantly across the 4 H levels (which it does), the regression model is misspecified because it ignores the primary driver of the t-statistic's distribution (the denominator's standard error, which depends on N_eff). The model should either include N_eff as a covariate or the design must explicitly vary N to observe the interaction. A simple bivariate regression of ErrorRate ~ H with fixed N is insufficient to validate the 'mechanism of failure' as claimed.
